# 2 Samuel Chapter 9 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 177v–178r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_009_page_001.jpg, 2SA_009_page_002.jpg

---

**1** David asked, "Is there anyone still left from Saul's family? I want to show them faithful love for Jonathan's sake."

**2** Now there was a servant of Saul's household named Ziba, and they brought him before David. "Are you Ziba?" the king asked. "At your service," he replied.

**3** The king said, "Is there no one left from Saul's family that I can show God's faithful love to?" Ziba told the king, "There is still one of Jonathan's sons — he's crippled in both feet."

**4** "Where is he?" the king asked. Ziba said, "He's in the home of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar."

**5** So King David sent for him and had him brought from Machir's house in Lo-debar.

**6** When Mephibosheth — the son of Jonathan, grandson of Saul — came before David, he fell face down and prostrated himself. "Mephibosheth!" David said. "I am your servant," he answered.

**7** "Don't be afraid," David told him. "I am determined to show you faithful love because of your father Jonathan. I will give back to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table."

**8** Mephibosheth bowed low and said, "Who am I that you would notice a dead dog like me?"

**9** Then the king called for Ziba, Saul's servant, and told him, "Everything that belonged to Saul and his entire family I have given to your master's grandson.

**10** You are to farm the land for him — you, your sons, and your servants — and bring in the harvest so that your master's family will have food. But Mephibosheth himself will always eat at my table." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

**11** "Your servant will do everything my lord the king commands," Ziba answered. And so Mephibosheth ate at David's table, just like one of the king's own sons.

**12** Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. Everyone living in Ziba's household served Mephibosheth.

**13** Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem from then on, because he always ate at the king's table. He was lame in both feet.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "faithful love":** The Hebrew *chesed* is the soul of this chapter. It means more than kindness — it is love bound by covenant, love that keeps its promises even when the person who extracted the promise is dead. David's question is not idle curiosity; it is a king searching for a way to honor a vow.

**Verse 4 — "Lo-debar":** The name of this town can be heard as "no-thing" or "no-word" in Hebrew. The grandson of a king is hiding in a place whose name means nowhere. The narrative geography is theology: *chesed* reaches into oblivion and brings the forgotten to the king's table.

**Verse 8 — "a dead dog like me":** In the ancient world, calling yourself a dog was extreme self-deprecation. A *dead* dog is something not even worth kicking. Mephibosheth is saying: I am less than nothing to you. And David's response — the table, the land, the honor — is the narrator's picture of what covenant-faithfulness looks like in action.

**Verse 13 — the final sentence:** The chapter closes with a striking detail: "He was lame in both feet." This is not an afterthought. The narrator wants you to see it — Mephibosheth at the king's table, his disability hidden beneath it. The table of the king is where brokenness is covered by grace. Many readers have seen in this an image of God's own hospitality.

*— PNEUMA*
